name: Bronchogen

lead: Bronchogen is a four-amino-acid peptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Leu) from Khavinson's bioregulator program, described as targeting bronchial and lung tissue. In longevity circles it is discussed for organ rejuvenation and healthier aging.

It is reported to stimulate differentiation markers in aged bronchial cell cultures and, in rats with an induced obstructive lung condition, to improve bronchial epithelium and reduce inflammation. A biophysical study reported it stabilises DNA against melting. Published studies are in rats and cell cultures; no human trial was found and no appearance use is documented.

paras: It is sold as a research peptide and discussed in short-course organ-bioregulator routines in longevity communities. Any effect is a hope tied to lung health and aging rather than to looks directly.
No human safety data are available. It is not an approved medicine.

angle.text: Bronchogen is a short peptide aimed at lung tissue, discussed in longevity circles as an organ-specific anti-aging peptide for healthier aging. Data are rat and cell studies only; no human trials and no appearance link are known.

lead: Bronchogen is a synthetic tetrapeptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Leu, AEDL) developed within Vladimir Khavinson's program on short peptide bioregulators at the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, and described by that program as the peptide directed at bronchial and lung tissue.[1] It appears in the looksmaxxing and longevity peptide world because it belongs to a family of Khavinson peptides, alongside epitalon, that some people use as part of anti-aging routines, with the chain of reasoning being healthier tissue, better aging and a younger overall presentation.

Published research on bronchogen is preclinical. Studies report that it stimulated differentiation markers in aged human bronchial cell cultures[2] and that, in rats with an obstructive lung condition induced by nitrogen dioxide, a month of treatment restored bronchial epithelium and reduced neutrophilic inflammation.[3][4] Biophysical work reports that it binds DNA and raises its melting temperature.[5] No human trial of bronchogen has been published, and no direct link to appearance is documented.
infobox: Khavinson group, St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology

paras: Bronchogen is a four-residue peptide made of alanine, glutamic acid, aspartic acid and leucine.[1] It belongs to the Khavinson family of short synthetic bioregulators, which the group sometimes calls cytogens and describes as tissue-specific: bronchogen for bronchial and lung tissue, and related peptides for other organs.[1] Epitalon (Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly) differs from bronchogen by one amino acid, and the two have been studied side by side in some experiments.[6]

Khavinson's group proposes that very short peptides can enter cells and nuclei and interact with DNA to modulate gene expression in a tissue-specific way, an idea described as epigenetic regulation.[1][7] A cell-culture study reported that fluorescent-labelled short peptides penetrated HeLa cell nuclei and interacted with oligonucleotides in a sequence-dependent way, and named bronchogen among the peptides that bind DNA.[7] A calorimetry study found that bronchogen raised the melting temperature of calf thymus and mouse liver DNA by 3.1 degrees C over a narrow range of molar ratios, which the authors read as DNA stabilisation.[5]

In cultures of human embryonic bronchial cells, expression of the differentiation factors CXCL12 and Hoxa3 declined in late-passage (aging) cells and was reported to be stimulated by bronchogen, with the effect more pronounced in aged cultures, which the authors proposed as a mechanism of a geroprotective effect.[2] The same study reported tissue-specific effects for related peptides: pancragen in pancreatic cells and vesugen in fibroblasts.[2]

In a rat model of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease created by 60 days of intermittent nitrogen dioxide exposure, one month of bronchogen was reported to remove features of epithelial remodelling, including goblet cell hyperplasia, squamous metaplasia, lymphocytic infiltration and emphysema, and to restore ciliated cells. Secretory IgA rose, and cytokine profiles in lavage fluid suggested less neutrophilic inflammation.[4] A second report from the group found restored bronchial epithelium and increased secretory IgA and surfactant protein B.[3]

Related peptides including bronchogen and epitalon also increased growth of tobacco callus cultures and altered expression of growth-regulating genes in the plant, an observation the authors link to a possible signalling role for short peptides.[6]

Vladimir Khavinson (1946 to 2024) was a Russian gerontologist who directed the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology and is credited with discovering and developing peptide bioregulators.[8] Wikipedia lists six peptide medicines permitted for medical use in the USSR and Russia, including thymalin, epithalamin and retinalamin, first used for military medical services, and notes that short synthetic di-, tri- and tetrapeptides were developed alongside organ extracts.[8] Bronchogen is one of the synthetic tetrapeptides in this family and is not among the listed approved preparations.[8]

Most published work on bronchogen comes from this one research group, a feature that reviewers of the peptide literature commonly note when considering how widely the findings have been reproduced; the Wikipedia page on Khavinson itself is tagged as containing promotional content, and its safety statements rest largely on the group's own studies.[8]

Bronchogen is sold as a research peptide and appears in discussions of Khavinson peptides in longevity circles, usually alongside epitalon.[1] It has no approved status as a medicine in the countries identified in the sources, and no clinical safety data in humans have been published.
